9. In the present suit, if the plaintiffs were minded to suppress notice of the suit by practicing fraud so that they could get an easy decree they should have suppressed notice on all the defendants who might have been expected to contest the suit, particularly Defendant No.1. It appears that all the defendants who are interested to defeat the claim of the plaintiff did appear in the, suit and one of them seriously contested by filing a written statement and by adducing evidence. Some others who are the brothers and sisters of the appellant petitioner appeared in the suit, admitted the allegations of the plaintiffs and prayed for sahams. It is difficult to imagine what conceivable motive the plaintiffs might have had to suppress the notice only upon Defendant No. 7 and not upon the others. Even the co-applicant of the application under Order 9 Rule 13 being her sister admitted that she had received the notice. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case we are definitely of opinion that there is no material on record from which an act of evil design of the plaintiffs could be inferred. We are there for of the view that the learned Subordinate Judges properly appreciated the evidence on record and rightly found that Defendant No.7 petitioner was aware of the decree from the very beginning. 

 23. The same question came up for consideration in the case of Monomohan Kundu Vs. Nripendra Nath Nandi and others before a, Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court consisting of Nasim Ali and Edgley JJ, reported in 41 C.W.N. 1271 same case A.I.R. 1937 Cal/548 same use 172 I. C.608, in which the ratio of the case was stated in the following words: 

 36. In the case of Mallin Lal Vs. Joytun which arose. out of a proceeding under section 96 .of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and was decided by Asir J, sitting singly, the learned Judge appears to have preferred the view of the Madras High Court and held that the trial Court can exercise the power under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside an exparte order even after the appeal which was preferred against the said order has been disposed of. It may be noted that the applicant in the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. and the appellant against the exparte order was the same person. It appears that the view of Hasan J, as expressed in 12 D.L.R. (Dacca) 581 was not brought to the notice of this Court. The reasoning of the learned Judge has been expressed in the following words: 

 37. In a subsequent case before another learned Single Judge, Sayem, J. (as his lord- ship then was) a similar question arose, but his lordship though inclined in favour of the view of the Madras High Court, was unable to agree with the view expressed in the case of Makhan Lal Dutra Vs. Joytun Bibi as the applicant himself was the appellant, and the matter was referred to a Division Bench consisting of Murshed C.J. and Abdullah J. and the said Bench has expressed itself in the said case, which has been reported has Atul Chandra Vs. Bhagabat Das and others in 18 D.L.R. (Dacca) 81, generally in favour of the view that the original court does not lose Jurisdiction to dispose of a proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code even after an appeal preferred against the said exparte decree has been disposed of by the appellate Court, although OD the facts of that case, the learned Judges were of the view that the defendants in question were not entitled to any relief in the proceeding under Order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. In the said case, a decree was passed ex parte against Defendants No. 4-7, on contest against Defendant Nos. 8 and 10 and without contest against the rest. Defendants Nos. 4 to 6 filled an application in the Trial Court under order 9 rule 13 C.P.C. to set aside the exparte decree and also filed an appeal against the said exparte decree. The appeal was heard before the disposal of the application under Order 9 rule 13 and was dismissed affirming he judgment of the Trial Court. The Misc. Case under Order 9 rule 13 in the meantime was dismissed for default but the petitioners preferred a Misc. Appeal as against the said order. The appellate Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that after the dismissal of the appeal against the decree, the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was no longer maintainable. The Division Bench, which ultimately heard the rule obtained under section 115 C.P. Code against the said order of dismissal, discharged it on the view that the petitioners had complete opportunity of mooting the points, raised by them in their written statement, in the appeal filed by them and that after having obtained an adverse decree the petitioners were not entitled to have this matter considered again. The learned Judges, however, even after dismissal of the application proceeded to discuss the question of law which according to them, was referred to the larger Bench because of the conflicting and some what rather irreconcilable decisions and proceeded to give their opinion on the question.
